title_en: The Rulings Concerning Women in Fasting
body_ar: بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم الحمد لله رب العالمين وأصلي وأسلم على من بعث رحمة للعالمين وعلى آله وأصحابه ومن اهتدى بهديه واستن بسنته إلى يوم الدين السلام عليكم ورحمة الله وبركاته، أما بعد فإن النساء يتميزن ببعض الأحكام المختصة، نظرا لأن الأحكام أحكام الشرع مبنية على مراعاة الفروق الفردية وعلى الرفق واللطف، وقد قال تعالى: {ما جعل عليكم في الدين من حرج}، والمشقة تجلب التيسير، وهي قاعدة عامة من القواعد الشرعية الكبرى، فكل ما فيه مشقة على الإنسان فالله تعالى يرفع فيه التكليف والحرج..
body_en:
In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds. I pray for blessing and peace upon the one who was sent as a mercy to the worlds, and upon his family and his Companions and all who are guided by his guidance and follow his practice until the Day of Judgement. Peace be upon you, and the mercy of God and His blessings.

To proceed: women are marked out by certain rulings particular to them, in view of the fact that the rulings — the rulings of the revealed law — are built upon taking account of individual differences, and upon gentleness and kindness. God, exalted, has said: {He has not placed upon you any hardship in religion} (Sūrat al-Ḥajj 22:78). And hardship brings ease: this is a general maxim, one of the great maxims of the revealed law. So everything in which there is hardship (mashaqqah) for a person, God, exalted, lifts the obligation and the constraint in it..

flags.arabic: فكل ما فيه مشقة على الإنسان فالله تعالى يرفع فيه التكليف والحرج..
flags.context: the sentence on which the published page breaks off
options: render faithfully, mark as an excerpt, and do not present it as a ruling
present it as the Sheikh's general ruling on hardship and obligation
flags.note: CRITICAL FOR DISPLAY — STYLE GUIDE §9 AND §10. Read alone, the closing sentence states, with no qualification at all, that God lifts obligation wherever there is hardship for a person. In the Sheikh's own technical vocabulary that is not what mashaqqah does — the glossary records that ḍarūrah is a technical threshold and ḥājah a lower one with different legal effect, and mashaqqah is ordinary hardship. The qualification is plainly in the part of the lecture that the page does not publish. The page breaks off on a double full stop before a single ruling concerning women is given, which is the whole of what the title promises. The site must not render this as a fatwa.

One of the five great maxims of the schools (al-qawāʿid al-fiqhiyyah al-kubrā). It is a fixed technical formula and will recur across the corpus, so a standard English rendering should be fixed now rather than per article. 'Hardship brings ease' is the most current English form.

flags.arabic: نظرا لأن الأحكام أحكام الشرع مبنية على
flags.context: the opening clause of the substantive paragraph
options: read as dittography and render once, as done here
read الأحكام أحكام الشرع as a deliberate appositional emphasis
flags.note: SOURCE DEFECT. The phrase الأحكام أحكام الشرع repeats al-aḥkām, most likely a transcription slip from the spoken original or a copying error. The repetition is preserved in body_ar; the English renders it as an apposition ('the rulings — the rulings of the revealed law —') rather than silently dropping one of them.

Qur'anic and hadith renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic.
The opening is the khuṭbat al-ḥājah, the standard formula with which the Sheikh begins a lecture. It is rendered in full rather than abbreviated, since it is part of the text as published.

EXCERPT ONLY. The page publishes the opening of the lecture and breaks off; the full text sits behind the .docx download recorded in source_download_link. The English ends exactly where the Arabic ends and the thought has not been completed. The site must render this with an excerpt banner and never as a whole article.
The Qur'anic quotation is given in the source without a reference; the reference has been supplied per house style. The wording matches Sūrat al-Ḥajj 22:78.
This record is a lecture opening, not a fatwa, and is typed transcript for that reason.
Nothing of the Sheikh's actual treatment of women and fasting is present in the published text; the English adds nothing to fill that gap.
